lead: Maxwell's four equations are the complete bookkeeping of classical electricity and magnetism: charges make D, there are no magnetic charges, changing B makes E, and currents or changing D make H. The fourth equation exists because Ampere's law alone fails at a charging capacitor; a displacement current I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt repairs it. These equations predict electromagnetic waves, so they sit under radio, mobile phones, radar, UPI card readers and every antenna.
prereq: You need: Gauss's law (3.3), D and polarization (3.5), Ampere's law (3.6) and Faraday's law (3.7).

sections.h3: The four equations, in two forms

blocks.text: Write the laws for free charge and free current in matter. The electric displacement D (C/m²) and magnetic field strength H (A/m) absorb the dielectric and magnetic response; E is electric field (V/m), B is magnetic flux density (T), ρ_free is free charge density (C/m³), and J is free current density (A/m²).
∮ D·dS = Q_free,enc; ∮ B·dS = 0; ∮ E·dl = −d/dt ∫ B·dS; ∮ H·dl = I_free,enc + d/dt ∫ D·dS
blocks.where: S is a closed surface for the first two and an open surface bounded by loop C for the last two; Q_free,enc and I_free,enc are free charge and free current enclosed; dS is the outward vector surface element and dl is the line element.

blocks.text: In differential form, ∇·D = ρ_free, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t. The names are Gauss for E, Gauss for B (no magnetic monopoles), Faraday, and Ampere–Maxwell.

The first and second are scalar statements about sources. The third and fourth are vector statements about circulation. Together they fix E and B everywhere once sources and boundary values are given.

sections.h3: The capacitor problem and displacement current

blocks.text: Take a capacitor charging through a wire. Choose a loop C around the wire and a surface S bounded by C. If S is the flat disc cutting the wire, Ampere's law gives ∮H·dl = I. If S is a balloon that passes through the capacitor gap, no conduction current crosses it, so the same law gives zero. The loop C is the same; the answer cannot depend on the surface.

Maxwell repaired this by adding the displacement current. The general displacement current through the chosen surface is I_d = d/dt ∫ D·dS. In vacuum D = ε₀E, so this reduces to I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt with Φ_E = ∫E·dS (V·m).

blocks.where: I_d is displacement current (A); D is electric displacement (C/m²); S is the chosen open surface. In vacuum D = ε₀E, so I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt with Φ_E = ∫E·dS (V·m); ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m.

blocks.text: For the capacitor I_d = C dV/dt, where C is capacitance (F) and V is voltage (V). This equals the conduction current in the wire, so the full current I + I_d is continuous around the circuit.

The continuity equation follows: ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t. Free charge leaving a small volume equals the fall of charge inside it. Displacement current does not mean charge jumps the gap; it is a changing electric field that produces the same magnetic effect.

The four equations need links between D and E, B and H, and J and E. For a linear, isotropic medium these are D = ε₀ε<sub>r</sub> E, B = μ₀μ<sub>r</sub> H, J = σE. Here ε<sub>r</sub> is relative permittivity (no unit), μ<sub>r</sub> is relative permeability (no unit), σ is conductivity (S/m), μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m, and ε₀ is as above.

At an interface, integrate the equations over a thin pillbox or loop. Let n̂ point from medium 1 to medium 2. Then the tangential electric field is continuous, the normal D jumps by free surface charge ρ_s (C/m²), which some books call σ_f, the normal B is continuous, and the tangential H jumps by free surface current K (A/m).

Boundary condition
Meaning
rows: jump equals free surface charge ρ_s

blocks.text: If there is no free surface charge, D_n is continuous; if there is no free surface current, H_t is continuous. These conditions let you join fields across a dielectric, a metal surface or a magnetic material without solving the whole region at once.

The equations unify electricity, magnetism and optics. In free space J = 0 and ρ = 0, so the equations couple changing E and changing B. Taking the curl of Faraday's law and substituting Ampere–Maxwell gives a wave equation with speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 2.998×10⁸ m/s, the speed of light.

That prediction made light an electromagnetic wave. The same equations design antennas, transmission lines, microwave ovens, radar and wireless chargers. They also set the boundary conditions used in waveguides and optical fibres.

The displacement term is small at low frequency and large when fields change fast, so circuit theory works at 50 Hz while microwave design needs the full set. Maxwell's equations are four, but they contain all classical electric and magnetic facts once the medium relations are supplied. The next chapter solves the free-space wave equation. Reflection at surfaces uses the boundary conditions above and is treated in Unit 4.

figure.caption: The four laws are the complete set. The Ampere–Maxwell law, with the displacement term, closes the set; in free space the four laws combine into a wave equation.

spec.title: Four equations, one wave
spec.aria: The two Gauss laws, Faraday's law and the Ampere–Maxwell law are the complete set, and in free space they combine into a wave equation.

examples.question: A 1 nF parallel-plate capacitor has plate area 0.01 m² and is charged so that its voltage rises at dV/dt = 10⁶ V/s. Find the displacement current in the gap and the displacement-current density. State how it compares with the conduction current in the wire.
steps: Given C = 1 nF = 1×10⁻⁹ F, dV/dt = 10⁶ V/s, A = 0.01 m².
For a capacitor, the displacement current equals the charging current: I_d = C dV/dt.
The displacement-current density is J_d = I_d/A = (1×10⁻³ A)/(0.01 m²) = 0.1 A/m².
In the series circuit this equals the conduction current in the wire; the full current is continuous.
examples.answer: I_d = 1×10⁻³ A = 1 mA and J_d = 0.1 A/m²; both match the conduction current in the wire.

traps: Dropping ∂D/∂t at a capacitor: then Ampere's law gives different currents for a flat surface and a balloon surface.
Mixing boundary conditions: E_t is continuous, but D_n jumps by ρ_s; B_n is continuous, but H_t jumps by K.
Calling displacement current a flow of charge through the gap. It is a changing electric field; no charge crosses the dielectric.
Using D = ε₀E inside a dielectric with ε_r ≠ 1. Use D = ε₀ε_rE, and use free charge in ∇·D = ρ_free.
Forgetting the minus sign in Faraday's law: ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, not +∂B/∂t.

quiz.q: Write the four Maxwell equations in differential form for a medium with free charge and free current.
Why does Ampere's law alone fail for a charging capacitor?
quiz.a: A loop around the wire bounds both a disc cutting the wire and a balloon through the gap; the first encloses I, the second encloses 0, so ∮H·dl would depend on the chosen surface. The displacement term d/dt∫D·dS makes both give the same result.

quiz.q: A 2 nF capacitor with plate area 0.02 m² has dV/dt = 5×10⁵ V/s. Find I_d and J_d.
A boundary has no free surface charge but has a free surface current. Which components of E, D, B and H are continuous?
quiz.a: E_t is continuous; D_n is continuous because ρ_s = 0; B_n is continuous; H_t jumps by K, so H_t is not continuous.

quiz.q: State the constitutive relations for a linear medium and define each symbol.
quiz.a: D = ε₀ε_rE, B = μ₀μ_rH, J = σE; ε_r is relative permittivity, μ_r is relative permeability, σ is conductivity; ε₀ and μ₀ are vacuum constants.

quiz.q: What is the continuity equation and what does it say?
quiz.a: ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t; the divergence of free current density equals the rate at which free charge density falls.

quiz.q: In free space, which two Maxwell equations couple E and B in the wave equation?
quiz.a: Faraday ∇×E = −∂B/∂t and Ampere–Maxwell ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t with J = 0, D = ε₀E and B = μ₀H; taking the curl of one and substituting the other gives the wave equation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Maxwell's equations are solved numerically in finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) and finite-element codes to design mobile-phone antennas, MRI coils, radar absorbers and photonic chips. Engineers use impedance boundary conditions to replace a complicated metal or ground plane by a surface relation. Newer topics include metamaterials with negative ε_r and μ_r, transformation optics, and wireless power transfer. Search next for FDTD, impedance boundary condition and computational electromagnetics.
